domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk centers on Sierra's Agent Development Life Cycle methodology for building, testing, and iteratively refining autonomous agents in production. Sierra builds conversational AI agents for consumer brands handling customer support, sales, and subscription management across enterprise operations. The ADLC spans deployment, production iteration, and evaluation via Experience Manager QA pipelines with test creation and releases. Requires familiarity with SDLC and LLM properties but is accessible to practitioners building production agents. Recorded conference talk at the AI Engineer Summit 2025. All claims are directly stated in the transcript with supporting evidence anchors.

summary: Zack Reneau-Wedeen from Sierra presents "The Agent Development Life Cycle" at the AI Engineer Summit 2025 in New York. Sierra builds conversational AI agents for consumer brands including Sonos, ADT, SiriusXM, and Chubbies, expanding beyond chat-based customer service into phone interactions, sales, subscription management, and product recommendations. Zack traces AI's evolution from 2012, when Google Brain identified cats on YouTube with ~1 billion parameter models—roughly one-thousandth of today's ~1 trillion parameter frontier models—through 2016, when he worked on the first version of Google Lens. The talk's central case study is Chubbies, whose agent Duncan Smothers handles sizing, inventory, package tracking, and autonomous refunds with higher customer satisfaction. Sierra's philosophy treats every agent as a product requiring full developer and operations platforms, with forward-deployed agent engineering and PM teams. Zack contrasts LLMs (non-deterministic, slow, expensive, flexible, creative) with traditional software (deterministic, fast, cheap, rigid), describing building on LLMs as building on a foundation of jello. The Agent Development Life Cycle (ADLC) resembles the SDLC but emphasizes iterative refinement with customers in production. Quality assurance uses Sierra's Experience Manager: conversations are reviewed, issues filed, tests created, and releases made—agents grow from a handful of tests at launch to hundreds and thousands. Chubbies agents even have budgets to delight customers, such as door-dashing shorts from retail locations. A year ago this process was manual; now AI accelerates each stage. The ADLC is more effective at scale—Duncan handled hundreds of thousands of requests while some customers do tens of millions. External change comes from model upgrades, reasoning paradigms, and multimodality, with reasoning models as force multipliers across every step. Sierra launched voice generally available in October; SiriusXM, with tens of millions of US customers, uses voice to answer every call immediately. Zack frames voice like responsive web design—one agent codebase responsive across channels and modalities. He closes reflecting that LLMs remind us of humans—unpredictable, slow, bad at math—yet they enable empathetic design, letting builders put themselves in the agent's shoes.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Sierra Overview
sections.summary: Zack introduces himself and Sierra as a conversational AI platform for businesses, noting expansion from chat-based customer service to phone interactions, sales, subscription management, and product recommendations by end of 2025.

sections.title: 2016 AI Caves and Google Lens
sections.summary: Zack shares his 2016 experience at Google building the first version of Google Lens, distinguishing Chihuahuas from blueberry muffins. He describes testing early computer vision on walks in NYC, noting the slot-machine feeling of inconsistent AI results that resonates with current AI builders.

sections.title: Present-Day Google Lens and Iterative Improvement
sections.summary: Zack shows how Google Lens evolved over a decade to support shopping, translation, math homework, and flower identification, attributing success to consistent step-by-step iteration formalized in the software development life cycle.

sections.title: 2012 AI Era and Chubbies Origin
sections.summary: Zack recalls 2012 when Google Brain identified cats on YouTube with ~1 billion parameter models, roughly one-thousandth of today's frontier models. He connects this era to Marc Andreessen's software-eating-the-world essay and the founding of Chubbies with their contrarian idea about men's shorts.

sections.title: Chubbies Partnership and Duncan Smothers Demonstrations
sections.summary: Chubbies' SVP Kit Garten partnered with Sierra, creating agent Duncan Smothers. Zack demonstrates Duncan handling sizing and fit with product recommendations, inventory tracking, package tracking with multiple tracking numbers, and autonomous refund issuance. Results: more customers helped faster with higher satisfaction.

sections.title: Every Agent Is a Product
sections.summary: Sierra's philosophy treats every agent as a product requiring a fully featured developer platform and customer experience operations platform. Dedicated agent engineering and agent PM teams are forward-deployed with customers, working daily alongside teams like Kit's at Chubbies.

sections.title: AI Engineering World's Fair and Networking
sections.summary: Zack recounts meeting Shawn at the AI Engineering World's Fair in June during a Deepgram workshop, bonding over voice agent development tooling. Shawn later joined Sierra. Zack invites audience members to connect after the talk.

sections.title: LLMs vs Traditional Software and ADLC Introduction
sections.summary: Zack contrasts LLMs (non-deterministic, slow, expensive, flexible, creative, reasoning) with traditional software (deterministic, fast, cheap, rigid, if-statements). He describes building on LLMs as building on a foundation of jello and introduces the agent development life cycle as a methodology combining both strengths.

sections.title: ADLC Quality Assurance and Experience Manager
sections.summary: Zack details the ADLC, emphasizing iterative refinement with customers in production. Sierra's Experience Manager lets customer teams review conversations, view real-time reports, and file issues—e.g., Duncan making incomplete or timed-out API calls. Issues trigger test creation; passing tests enable releases. Agents grow from a handful of tests at launch to hundreds and thousands. Chubbies agents also have budgets to delight customers, such as door-dashing shorts from retail when unavailable online.

sections.title: AI-Accelerated ADLC and Scale Benefits
sections.summary: A year ago Sierra's ADLC was entirely manual; now AI accelerates each stage. The ADLC is more effective at scale—Duncan handled hundreds of thousands of requests while some customers do tens of millions. External change comes from model upgrades, reasoning paradigms, and multimodality, with reasoning models acting as force multipliers across development, testing, and QA.

sections.title: Voice Launch and SiriusXM
sections.summary: Sierra launched voice generally available in October. SiriusXM, with tens of millions of US customers, uses voice to pick up every call immediately. Zack frames voice like responsive web design—one agent codebase responsive across channels and modalities, with customization for phrasing and latency optimization, but working out of the box.

sections.title: Closing Reflections on LLMs and Empathy
sections.summary: Zack closes reflecting that LLMs remind us of humans—unpredictable, slow, bad at math—yet enable empathetic design, letting builders inhabit the agent's perspective. He poses the multimodal question: how would you perform responding from transcribed text with few hundred milliseconds of delay? Sierra is building more robust multimodal experiences by giving LLMs the same inputs humans have.
